1.e4 e5 2.f4.name: King's Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4.background: Ruy López de Segura was the first to publish analysis of it, and it already appears in Lucena's book of 1497. After losing to Spassky's King's Gambit at Mar del Plata in 1960, Fischer published “A Bust to the King's Gambit” the following year, claiming that it loses by force; the opening has been rare at the highest level since Rudolf Spielmann stopped playing it regularly.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4.strategy: Takes the pawn, the most testing reply: White has to prove the gambit with a lead in development and pressure on f7, while Black has to hold the extra pawn without falling behind. Black can either keep the pawn or give it back to speed up development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5.strategy: Declines the pawn and develops with a point: the bishop controls g1, so White cannot castle short, and it makes the d4 advance costly. Black settles for a quieter, roughly level game and avoids the sharpest gambit play; White must spend time to drive the bishop away.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5.strategy: Counterattacks the e4 pawn at once instead of taking or defending: Black wants quick development and an open centre, aiming at White's weakened kingside. Grabbing 3.fxe5 loses a rook to ...Qh4+ and ...Qxe4+.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6.name: King's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and guards e5, but takes no stand on the centre or the f4 pawn: Black declines without making a claim. White keeps the choice between sharp and quiet play, and the move is far more common among club players than in master games.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nf6.name: King's Gambit Declined: Petrov's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nf6.background: The move was suggested by Petroff.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hits e4, so taking on e5 is answered by ...Nxe4 and the pawns balance again. The simplifying lines that follow tend to leave White a small, safe edge in the endgame, which makes this a modest way to decline.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+.name: King's Gambit Declined: Keene's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+.strategy: Checks at once, but the check is harmless: 3.g3 attacks the queen and also supports the f4 pawn, so the queen must retreat and Black has lost time for nothing. An early queen sortie gives White the lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6.name: King's Gambit Declined: Norwalde Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early to win the f4 pawn, but takes the best square from the king's knight and invites an attack on the queen: after 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.d4 the c1-bishop hits the queen while e5 is attacked too, and White gets a free centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Panteldakis Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5.background: One of the oldest countergambits to the King's Gambit, known from a game of Greco's from 1625. It is named after Peter Pantelidakis, an amateur who proposed it in Chess Life and Review.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5.strategy: A countergambit that hits e4 but opens Black's own king: 3.exf5 threatens Qh5+, and Black has no development to show for the loosened kingside. Black fights for the centre in the wrong place.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn but weakens the king and blocks the knight's best square. 3.fxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ forces the king to move (4...g6? 5.Qxe5+ wins the h8 rook), so Black loses a pawn and the right to castle.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 g5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Zilbermints Double Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 g5.strategy: Gives up a pawn for nothing: 3.fxg5 simply wins it, and 3...Qxg5? runs into 4.d4, when the c1-bishop attacks the queen and e5 is attacked too. Black's kingside is wrecked without any return.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: it covers h4, so the ...Qh4+ trick no longer works, and it makes the threat of fxe5 real since e5 is attacked twice. White develops with a threat and prepares to build a central pawn mass.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Qh5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation, Walthoffen Attack
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Qh5.strategy: An early queen raid on e5 and f7. It threatens the pawn, but ...Nf6 attacks the queen with a developing move, so White wins the pawn at best at the cost of time and an exposed queen.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Bc4.strategy: Brings the bishop to its best diagonal at once, eyeing f7, but neglects the centre: Black strikes with ...d5, attacking the bishop and the e4 pawn together. White can win the d5 pawn, but Black develops with gain of time and has at least an even game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6.strategy: The standard defence of e5: a pawn holds it, the c8-bishop is freed, and the bishop on c5 keeps its grip on g1. Black accepts a slightly passive position for a sound structure and waits to see how White uses the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 g5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Senechaud Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 g5.strategy: Counterattacks f4 at once, but 4.fxg5 wins a pawn, since 4...Qxg5? loses the queen to Nxg5. The g-pawn also shuts Black's own queen out of h4 and loosens the kingside for nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops, but defends e5 only once while White attacks it twice: 4.fxe5 wins a pawn, and Black gets only a speculative queen raid on h4 in return.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3.strategy: Prepares to strike with the d-pawn, which would attack the bishop and e5 together and give White a broad pawn centre. The cost is time and the c3 square for the queen's knight; if Black fights back at once, the centre becomes a target rather than a strength.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and guards e4, and from c3 the knight can head for a4 to challenge the bishop that stops White castling. White chooses piece play over an immediate pawn centre and plays against the c5-bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.b4.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation, Rotlewi Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.b4.strategy: Offers a pawn to deflect the bishop and gain time with c3 for a strong centre. It costs a pawn and loosens the queenside, and Black can take it and retreat safely, so it is a rare, slightly dubious choice.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.fxe5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical, Soldatenkov Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.fxe5.strategy: Gives up the tension at once, trading White's f-pawn for Black's e-pawn. The pawn on e5 is poisoned for now: 5.Nxe5? Qh4+ 6.g3 Qxe4+ forks the knight and the h1 rook. The game loses most of the gambit's attacking spirit.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4.strategy: Develops with a pin: the f3 knight, which attacks e5 and watches d4, is tied to the queen, so White's central plan loses some support. White answers by resolving the tension in the centre before anything else.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 f5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation, Rubinstein Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 f5.strategy: Meets the gambit with a countergambit of its own: Black fights for e4 at once. It opens the diagonal in front of the king, though, and leaves Black's pawns on e5 and f5 as targets, so it is an offbeat try rather than a main line.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which nothing guards since the pawn on c3 blocks the knight's natural square, and so makes White's plan of a broad pawn centre costly: a recapture on d4 comes with a check on b4. Black keeps a compact, flexible position and leaves White to commit first.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bb6.strategy: Steps the bishop out of range of a coming central advance while keeping it on the diagonal aimed at f2. It is solid, but it costs a tempo and does nothing for development, so White gets time to build a full centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4 5.fxe.strategy: Takes on e5 so that Black must recapture with the d-pawn, leaving the e5 pawn without a defender once the pinned knight is free. White gives up the f-pawn and the gambit's tension for open lines and the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4 5.Be2.strategy: Meets the pin the quiet way: the bishop guards the pinned knight, so a trade on f3 is answered with a recapture by a piece and White keeps the two bishops. It makes no threat, though, and leaves the centre tension where it is, so Black gets time to develop.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4 5.h3.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once: Black either gives up the bishop for the knight, which hands White the two bishops, or retreats and loses time. The move spends a tempo on the edge pawn and does nothing for the centre while the e5 pawn still stands.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4 5.fxe.strategy: The natural recapture: it wins the pawn back at once and keeps the bishop pinning the knight to the queen. The e5 pawn has no defender, though, so Black must be ready for White to break the pin with tempo and attack it, and the open centre rewards the better-developed side.

Trades the bishop for the knight before White can break the pin, which gives White the two bishops. After the recapture on f3 and ...dxe5, a bishop on c4 aims at f7 with the queen behind it, so Black must spend time on defence. Sound, but passive.
Develops but ignores the pawn that White has just won: White keeps it with 6.exd6 and stays a clean pawn up, with the pinned knight soon free again.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4 5.fxe.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation, Euwe Attack
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 Bg4 5.fxe.strategy: Breaks the pin with check: the queen leaves d1 with tempo, so the f3 knight is free again and e5 is a target. Black has to meet the check and the threat to e5 at once, and White takes over the initiative.

Develops and puts the bishop behind the knight, so a trade on f3 is recaptured by a piece. It makes no threat of its own, though the knight still eyes the loose e5 pawn, and Black has time to defend it and develop.

Develops the bishop with the e4 pawn guarded, so a trade on f3 is recaptured by the queen and White keeps the two bishops. It makes no threat and leaves the pin in place, so Black gets time to develop.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 f5 5.fxe5.strategy: Takes the e5 pawn and keeps the initiative: the pawn on f5 and the open diagonal in front of the king become the things to attack. White trades a gambit pawn for open lines and play against the loosened king.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 f5 5.d4.strategy: Strikes at the bishop and the e5 pawn at once, going for a broad pawn centre before the countergambit is consolidated. The move is double-edged: the centre is big, but Black's f5 pawn presses on e4 and the position opens quickly.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 f5 5.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn that pressed on e4, but spends a move on a pawn trade while the d-pawn and the f1-bishop stay at home. Black can hit the knight with the e-pawn, gaining time, or retake with the bishop at once, and has the easier development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.c3 f5 5.fxe5.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn and keeps the f5 pawn pressing on e4. The price is that the e5 pawn is attacked by the knight with no pawn to guard it, and the diagonal in front of Black's king stays open.

Counterattacks the knight before recapturing, so the e5 pawn stays on the board with the d6 pawn in its sights. It gives White more choices than the plain recapture and leads to a messier game, with the e4 pawn exposed.
Develops but leaves the pawn on e5 alone: White keeps the extra pawn by taking on d6, and Black has nothing to show for it.
Gains time by attacking the bishop and the e5 pawn at once, so the pawn centre grows with tempo. White opens the centre while Black's king still has an open diagonal in front of it.

Takes the pawn that pressed on e4 and opens the e-file, but it costs a move while the d-pawn and the f1-bishop stay at home. Black can hit the knight with the e-pawn, gaining time, or retake with the bishop at once.
Checks at once, but gains nothing: Black blocks with a developing move or a useful pawn move, and the queen stands offside while the d-pawn and the bishop are still at home.

Captures instead of retreating, giving back the centre pawn to keep the bishop active: after cxd4 it can check from b4. White gets a broad pawn centre, Black active pieces and the f5 pawn pressing e4, so the game turns on whether that centre is strong or overextended.

Counterattacks the knight instead of saving the bishop, which leads to a sharp exchange of pieces and queens. Material stays level, but Black's king is left in the centre without the right to castle, so the line is riskier than it needs to be.

Retreats the bishop but gives up the e5 pawn without a fight: it is attacked by the d-pawn and the knight with no defender, and White wins it with the queens facing each other on the open d-file. Black has to hit back at once on e4.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.Nc3 Nd7.name: King's Gambit Declined: Classical, Hanham Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.Nc3 Nd7.strategy: Defends e5 a second time with a piece and prepares to bring out the king's knight. It is compact but passive: the knight blocks the c8-bishop, and Black stays a little cramped.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a hit on e4, a pawn that only the c3-knight guards, so White must keep an eye on the centre while Black gets quick development. The bishop stays on its diagonal toward f2 and e5 is held firmly, a sound way to meet the gambit without giving up the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Bc5 3.Nf3 d6 4.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and adds a second defender to e5, with d4 and b4 under watch so White cannot build a centre for free. It is solid and active, though it blocks the c-pawn and commits the knight early.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5.strategy: The reply that refutes the countergambit: White wins the pawn and threatens Qh5+, because the f-pawn has left Black's king without cover on that diagonal. Black has to deal with the check while still a pawn down.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and covers h4, so Black's queen has no check there, and adds a second attacker to e5. It leaves the pawn on f5 alone, so Black can capture in the centre at once, and White gives up the clear edge that exf5 gives.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards the e4 pawn, but passes over both the pawn on f5 and the open diagonal to Black's king. Black can capture in the centre at once, and White settles for a balanced fight instead of the clear edge that exf5 gives.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4.strategy: The natural recapture: Black wins back the pawn and opens the e-file. But the diagonal to Black's king is still open, so White gets a check at once and Black has to answer threats instead of building in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 Qh4+.name: King's Gambit Declined: Panteldakis Countergambit, Greco Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 Qh4+.strategy: Gains a tempo with check, but the early queen sortie loses time rather than winning it: g3 blocks the check and attacks the queen, and White keeps the extra pawn with a comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 Bc5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Panteldakis Countergambit, Schiller's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop but does nothing about the threat: Qh5+ forces the king to move, losing castling, or the g-pawn to block, and White is a pawn up with the e5 pawn also attacked.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+.strategy: Cashes in the open diagonal at once: the check forces Black to weaken the kingside with the g-pawn or to move the king and forfeit castling. White keeps the initiative, at the cost of an early queen sortie.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3.strategy: A calmer route: the knight develops and covers h4, so Black's queen has no check there, and the f4 pawn can be won back once the c1-bishop is freed. White trades the immediate check for sound development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qe2+.strategy: Checks along the e-file and invites a queen trade, but Black can block with a developing bishop or with the queen at no cost. White spends a tempo and gives up the kingside attack that Qh5+ starts, for a quieter game with the f5 and f4 pawns facing each other.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal onto f5, so White's f5 pawn is attacked at once. Black wants to regain the pawn and hold the centre rather than defend passively.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece, but neither wins back the f5 pawn nor protects the f4 pawn, which a quick d4 attacks with the c1-bishop. Black's pawn problems are only postponed.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 Qe7+.strategy: Checks on the e-file, but White blocks with Be2, a developing move, and Black's queen now stands in front of its own bishop and knight. The check gains nothing, costs time on queen moves, and the pawn on f5 stays.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5 5.d.strategy: Claims the centre and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal onto the f4 pawn, so Black has to defend it. The f5 pawn is still attacked by the c8-bishop, and White accepts a balanced, symmetrical fight over both pawns.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5 5.B.strategy: Checks and develops the bishop, but Black blocks with a useful move: ...c6 even attacks the bishop and forces it back. White has spent time on a check that wins nothing, while the c8-bishop keeps its eye on the f5 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5 5.N.strategy: Develops and attacks the d5 pawn, but the queen defends it, and Black simply takes the f5 pawn with the c8-bishop. Material is level and White has not yet claimed the centre, so Black gets the comfortable side of a balanced game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5 5.d.strategy: Defends the f4 pawn with a developing move and mirrors White's set-up. The f5 pawn is still attacked by the c8-bishop, so White has to react to that before anything else.
Develops and covers h5 and e4, but leaves the f4 pawn to the c1-bishop, whose diagonal has just opened. Black then regains the f5 pawn and the pawns end level in an open game.
Takes the f5 pawn at once, but leaves the f4 pawn unprotected, and the c1-bishop takes it, so the pawns end level. Black has spent a move to reach a balanced game and given up the hold on f4.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5 5.d.name: King's Gambit Declined: Panteldakis Countergambit, Symmetrical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Nf3 d5 5.d.strategy: Develops and guards the f5 pawn, so taking it now just loses a bishop for a pawn. Both sides hold a pawn on the fifth and fourth rank in mirrored set-ups, and the game turns on who finishes development and breaks in the centre first.

Checks first, but Black answers with a useful move, and after ...c6 the bishop has to retreat, usually to d3, where it could have gone at once. White gains nothing from the check and gives Black the c6 pawn for free.

Guards the f5 pawn with the queen, so ...Bxf5 loses a bishop for a pawn. But the queen takes the best square from the f1-bishop and stands where Black's checks gain time, so White holds the pawn at a cost in development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+ g6.strategy: Blocks the check and keeps the right to castle, at the price of a pawn: White can take on g6, and Black's kingside is left open to the queen. Black counts on the tempo it can win with the queen in return.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+ Ke7.name: King's Gambit Declined: Panteldakis Countergambit, Shirazi Line
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+ Ke7.strategy: The main answer: the king steps to e7 and Black keeps the pawns level instead of giving a pawn away on g6. It costs castling and leaves the king in the middle, so White gets a lead in development and a lasting initiative, and Black has to untangle with care.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+ g6 5..strategy: Takes the pawn and leaves White a pawn up, with the g-pawn now attacking h7. Black cannot recapture with the h-pawn: it would open the h-file and Qxh8 would win the rook. Black must look for counterplay with a check instead.

Escapes the attack of the g6 pawn with a check and keeps fxg6 in hand. But Black blocks with ...Be7, and after fxg6 hxg6 has won back the pawn with the queens still on, which fxg6 at once does not allow.
Takes the pawn with the queen, but the h7 pawn recaptures and White has given the queen for a pawn.

Checks along the open e-file, which makes White block or move the king, and so wins back time for the pawn. This is the point of ...g6: the queen comes out with tempo while the h-pawn recapture, which would lose the rook, stays unplayed.

Attacks the queen, so gxh7+ now fails to ...Nxh5, and moves the g8 knight out of the pawn's reach. Black stays a pawn down with the g6 pawn cramping the kingside, but has a developed piece and a tempo against the queen.
Recaptures the pawn but opens the h-file: Qxh8 wins the rook, and the queen then attacks the knight on g8 as well.
Develops and eyes b2 but ignores the pawn on g6: gxh7+ is a discovered check from the queen, and once the king steps aside the pawn takes the knight on g8.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+ g6 5..name: King's Gambit Declined: Panteldakis Countergambit, Pawn Sacrifice Line
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f5 3.exf5 exf4 4.Qh5+ g6 5..strategy: Keeps the queens on and the pawn on g6 by moving the king instead of blocking. White gives up castling and the king sits uncomfortably on d1, so safety has been traded for material and White must consolidate quickly.

Meets the check by offering the queens, which ends the attack on White's king. After ...Qxe2+ the knight recaptures and hits the f4 pawn while the g6 pawn still threatens h7, so Black cannot win back g6 without losing f4. White stays a pawn up.

Blocks with the bishop, which keeps castling in reserve, but the bishop is pinned to the king by the queen, and White's own queen remains a target for ...Nf6. White keeps the extra pawn at the price of an awkward, undeveloped position.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.fxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn and punishes the weakening 2...f6. Recapturing with the f-pawn would be a blunder: Qh5+ g6 and Qxe5+ forks king and h8 rook. White gains a pawn and open lines at little risk.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and adds a second attacker to e5, which White can capture next move. The f6 pawn already blocks Black's queen from h4 and denies the knight its natural square, so White has no need to watch h4 and Black must deal with e5 at once.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards e4 while keeping the tension on e5. Black's f-pawn is awkwardly placed, which denies Black ...Nf6 and ...Qh4+, and the open diagonal to the king keeps Qh5+ in reserve, so White can afford to wait.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.fxe5 Nc6.name: King's Gambit Declined: Soller-Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.fxe5 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the pawn on e5 a second time and develops, so White must defend it or give it back. The knight also covers e5, which takes the sting out of Qh5+. Black gambits a pawn for quick development and play against White's centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.fxe5 fxe5.strategy: Recaptures with the f-pawn, which leaves the long diagonal to h8 open: Qh5+ g6 and Qxe5+ checks the king and attacks the rook on h8 at once, so Black loses the rook.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 f6 3.fxe5 d6.strategy: Stays a pawn down: Black only prepares to recapture with a developing move when White takes again. White keeps the clean extra pawn, and Black has little to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, covers h4 so Black's queen gets no check there, and threatens to win the e5 pawn by capturing on it. This is the standard way to meet the knight development, as in many King's Gambit lines.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and guards e4, a calmer way to play the gambit than hurrying the king's knight out. With the knight already on c6, Black can take on f4 without being driven back by an e-pawn push, so White gives up the direct pressure on e5 and plays for development and the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 at once, but leaves e5 alone and lets Black take on f4, after which White must spend a move stopping ...Qh4+. The pawn is given up for quick development and pressure on f7, and Black is the one with the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 f5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Miles Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 f5.background: Tony Miles advocated this countergambit, which is also known as the Adelaide Countergambit.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 f5.strategy: Counterattacks at once instead of defending the e5 pawn, and invites White to take it in return for open lines and activity. It is the usual practical idea here, but Black must play energetically to justify the risk.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Zilbermints Double Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5.strategy: Piles on f4, but leaves both e5 and g5 attacked twice and defended once, so White simply takes a pawn with fxg5 and keeps the better position. A speculative double gambit that pays too little for the material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Counters in the centre at once instead of defending e5: Black challenges e4, and if White takes, the queen recaptures in the middle, where White's knight can only chase it away with a gain of time. The game opens quickly and Black's pieces become as active as White's, which is the point of declining the gambit this way.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 exf4.strategy: Takes the gambit pawn with the knight already developed, a waiting approach that does nothing about White's plan to build the centre. Black keeps the extra pawn for the moment, but the knight on c6 becomes a target for White's d-pawn, so White gets the centre the gambit was played for.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.fxg5.strategy: Accepts the gambit by capturing. The new pawn on g5 is guarded by the f3-knight, so Black's queen cannot take it, and White is a pawn up with the f-file opened. White's task is to survive the early pressure and finish development.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.fxe5.strategy: Takes the e-pawn instead of the g-pawn, but ...g4 hits the f3-knight at once, and when it moves the knight on c6 takes the e5 pawn back. White has swapped the f-pawn for the e-pawn, gained nothing for the loosened position and lost time.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre and attacks e5 a third time instead of taking material. It is playable, but it leaves both pawn offers unresolved: the g5 pawn can still gain time against the f3-knight, and White gives up the clean extra pawn that the capture on g5 wins.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.fxg5 h6.name: King's Gambit Declined: Hobbs-Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.fxg5 h6.strategy: Challenges the g5 pawn at once, the point of the second pawn offer: if White takes on h6, Black recaptures with the rook or the bishop and gets an open file or diagonal against the kingside. Black is a pawn down and plays for speed of development, not for material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.fxg5 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a post where it supports e5 and prepares to win the g5 pawn back with ...h6. Black is a pawn down, but the pieces come out quickly and the pawn centre stays intact.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g5 4.fxg5 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, but does nothing about the g5 pawn. White consolidates and keeps the extra pawn, while Black has only a slightly freer game to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and guards e4, leaving the gambit pawn on f4 to the queen. White is happy to pay it: a queen that takes becomes a target for White's developing moves, and the tempi they gain are worth more than the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight with an attack on e5 and covers h4. The e4 pawn is not yet protected and comes under attack after ...Qxf4, so White must spend a move defending it; the lead in development has to pay for the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.fxe5.strategy: Takes the e5 pawn, but the queen recaptures on e5 with an attack on the loose e4 pawn, so White has to defend it at once. Material is level and the f-file is open, but Black's queen stands in the centre and is the more active piece.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4.strategy: Takes the pawn the gambit offered and keeps it, the most direct reply. But the queen has now moved twice and stands where White's developing moves attack it with tempo, so Black must prove that the extra pawn is worth the time lost. White's compensation is the lead in development and the central play.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 exf4.strategy: Takes the gambit pawn with the e-pawn so that the queen keeps its post, but gives up Black's pawn centre. 4.Nd5 attacks the queen at once and the f4 pawn with it, so Black loses time and the extra pawn is soon in danger.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds a defender to e5, but leaves the queen on f6, where a knight jump to d5 attacks it with tempo. Black has neither solved the problem of the f4 pawn nor found a safe post for the queen, and White's pieces come out with a gain of time.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.d4.name: King's Gambit Declined: Norwalde Variation, Schubert Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a gain of time: the pawn opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, so the queen on f4 is attacked and has to leave, and e4 stays guarded by the knight. Black keeps the extra pawn, but White gets the broad centre the gambit was played for.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the e5 pawn, tying the queen to its defence. It does not chase the queen at once, though, so Black gets time for a developing counter against the e4 pawn, which depends on the knight on c3.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nge2.strategy: Attacks the queen with a developing move, but the knight on e2 blocks the king's bishop and leaves h4 uncovered, so Black can check on h4 before retreating. White develops without taking the centre, and the queen escapes at no cost.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nf3 Bb4.strategy: Develops with a threat: if the bishop takes the knight, e4 loses its guard and the queen can take it with check. Black uses the time the queen was not chased to attack the piece that holds White's centre together, and keeps the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and supports e5, but leaves the queen on f4, where d4 attacks it at once with the c1-bishop, since the c3 knight guards e4. White gets the centre with a gain of time and Black's extra pawn comes under pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nf3 Qf6.strategy: Retreats the queen to a safe square and keeps the extra pawn, but it is the queen's third move in as many turns while White develops. The lead in development and the centre are the price of the pawn, so this is a safe but passive way to hold it.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nf3 Bb4 5..name: King's Gambit Declined: Norwalde Variation, Bücker Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qf6 3.Nc3 Qxf4 4.Nf3 Bb4 5..strategy: A second pawn offered on top of the first: the bishop develops and eyes f7, but it leaves e4 to fall with check after ...Bxc3. White has to hope that the lead in development and the pressure on f7 are worth two pawns.

Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal to the queen, so taking on c3 no longer wins the e4 pawn and the queen has to move with tempo against it. White holds the centre together and develops with gain of time; the pawn is the price.

Develops the bishop to a square where it guards e4, so ...Bxc3 no longer wins a pawn. If Black takes, the recapture with the d-pawn opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against the queen. The bishop blocks the d-pawn, though, so White's centre takes longer to form.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.g3.name: King's Gambit Declined: Keene's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.g3.strategy: Blocks the check and attacks the queen at once, so Black has wasted a move and the queen must run. The f4 pawn is now guarded and shields e4 from the queen along the rank; the squares around the king are looser, but Black has no pieces out to use them.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling and walks the king into the open while Black's queen is already active. Black simply takes the f4 pawn, the queen eyes e4 with check, and White has no piece out to help the king.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.g3 Qe7.name: King's Gambit Declined: Keene Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.g3 Qe7.strategy: Retreats to a square where the queen still guards e5 and keeps the f4 pawn under pressure. Black has lost time with the early check, and White's lead in development gives a small edge, but nothing is lost yet; the queen does block the king's bishop, so development has to be arranged around it.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.g3 Qf6.strategy: Keeps e5 defended and, together with the e-pawn, puts the f4 pawn under double attack, while the king's bishop keeps its diagonal. White must meet the threat to f4, and the queen on f6 can be hit by a knight jump later.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 Qh4+ 3.g3 Qd8.strategy: Retreats all the way and drops the e5 pawn: nothing defends it, and White takes it at once with the f-pawn. Black has lost two moves for nothing and is a pawn down with White's pieces still to develop.
